cards.front: A {{c1::checkpoint}} is a control mechanism that enforces dependency between cell-cycle events.
cards.back: It makes one event wait until another is finished.
cards.quote: A checkpoint is a control mechanism that enforces dependency between cell-cycle events.
cards.section: The idea: a checkpoint makes one event wait for another

cards.front: Irradiated rad9 budding yeast do not delay in G2. When a microtubule poison holds them in G2 for several hours, they repair the damage efficiently. What does this show about Rad9?
cards.back: Rad9 is needed for waiting, not for repair. Supplying the delay from outside rescued repair, so control and repair are separable.
cards.quote: When a microtubule poison held irradiated rad9 cells in G2 for several hours, repair could occur efficiently.
cards.section: The idea: a checkpoint makes one event wait for another

cards.front: In the rad9 yeast experiment, what result would have pointed to RAD9 being a repair gene, and why would it not have proved it?
cards.back: The held cells still failing to repair. That would point to repair but not prove it: the block might have been too short, or the damage beyond repair.
cards.why: More time rescues means a waiting defect; no rescue means perhaps a repair defect.
cards.quote: Had the held cells still failed to repair, that would have pointed to repair, though not proved it
cards.section: The idea: a checkpoint makes one event wait for another

cards.front: A checkpoint is a brake wired to a sensor. What kinds of unfinished job does the sensor detect, and what does the brake restrain?
cards.back: A broken DNA end, a stretch of single-stranded DNA, or an unattached kinetochore. It restrains the next transition's regulators: particular cyclin-CDKs, or APC/C-Cdc20-dependent destruction of securin and cyclin B.
cards.quote: A checkpoint is a brake wired to a sensor.
cards.section: The idea: a checkpoint makes one event wait for another

cards.front: Name the two ways a cell-cycle transition is made hard to undo, with an example of each.
cards.back: Destroying proteins that must then be made again (securin and cyclin B at anaphase, Sic1 at yeast G1/S), or flipping a positive-feedback switch that resists reversal (Cdk1 at entry into mitosis).
cards.quote: Depending on the step, it destroys proteins (securin and cyclin B at anaphase, Sic1 at yeast G1/S), which must be made again
cards.section: The idea: a checkpoint makes one event wait for another

cards.front: Cdk1's inhibitory phosphates are added by the kinases {{c1::Wee1 and Myt1}} and removed by Cdc25 phosphatases.
cards.back: The cell enters mitosis only when the Cdc25 side wins.
cards.quote: For Cdk1, the kinases Wee1 and Myt1 add those phosphates and Cdc25 phosphatases remove them.
cards.section: The map: three checkpoints, two engines

cards.front: What activator does the ubiquitin ligase APC/C need to pick its mitotic targets?
cards.back: Cdc20.
cards.quote: To pick its mitotic targets it needs the activator Cdc20.
cards.section: The map: three checkpoints, two engines

cards.front: A budding-yeast mad mutant is grown under ideal conditions, then under conditions where spindle assembly is slow. Predict its phenotype in each.
cards.back: Ideal: it often grows normally. Slow spindle: it moves on anyway, and the cost shows up as broken or missing chromosomes in the next generation.
cards.why: A checkpoint mutant divides on time instead of on completion. This holds for the classic yeast mutants, not every checkpoint protein.
cards.quote: A yeast rad9, mad or bub mutant often grows normally when nothing goes wrong.
cards.section: The map: three checkpoints, two engines

cards.front: Which complex binds the ends of a DNA double-strand break, and which kinase does it recruit?
cards.back: The MRN complex (Mre11, Rad50 and Nbs1); it recruits ATM.
cards.quote: The MRN complex (Mre11, Rad50 and Nbs1) binds the ends and recruits the kinase ATM.
cards.section: Damage and replication: kinases that keep a CDK off

cards.front: Which protein coats single-stranded DNA, and which kinase and partner does it help bring in?
cards.back: RPA, the single-strand binding protein; it helps bring in ATR with its partner ATRIP.
cards.quote: RPA helps bring in the kinase ATR with its partner ATRIP.
cards.section: Damage and replication: kinases that keep a CDK off

cards.front: In the DNA checkpoints, ATM mainly switches on the messenger kinase {{c1::Chk2}}, and ATR mainly switches on Chk1.
cards.quote: Each switches on a smaller messenger kinase: ATM mainly Chk2, ATR mainly Chk1.
cards.section: Damage and replication: kinases that keep a CDK off

cards.front: Why does single-stranded DNA appear at a stalled replication fork?
cards.back: The polymerase stops but the helicase keeps unwinding, leaving unpaired single strands.
cards.quote: Single strands appear at a stalled replication fork, when the polymerase stops but the helicase keeps unwinding.
cards.section: Damage and replication: kinases that keep a CDK off

cards.front: A double-strand break in S or G2 activates ATR as well as ATM. How?
cards.back: ATM promotes trimming of the broken ends, started by the Mre11 nuclease. Trimming exposes single strands, RPA coats them, and ATR joins in.
cards.quote: Trimming exposes single strands, RPA coats them, and ATR joins in.
cards.section: Damage and replication: kinases that keep a CDK off

cards.front: Is reaching RPA-coated DNA enough to switch ATR on? What else is needed?
cards.back: No. The protein TopBP1 strongly stimulates ATR's kinase activity, and ETAA1 can do so too.
cards.quote: Reaching the DNA is not enough to switch ATR on: the protein TopBP1 strongly stimulates its kinase activity, and ETAA1 can do so too.
cards.section: Damage and replication: kinases that keep a CDK off

cards.front: After DNA damage in G2, Chk1 and Chk2 inhibit the Cdc25 phosphatases. Predict what happens to Cdk1 and to the cell, and whether this brake can lift without new protein.
cards.back: Cdk1 keeps its inhibitory phosphates and stays off, so the cell waits in G2. Nothing was destroyed, so the brake can lift once the signal stops.
cards.why: The brake is a shift in the phosphate balance between Wee1/Myt1 and Cdc25.
cards.quote: Cdk1 keeps its inhibitory phosphates and stays off, so the cell waits in G2.
cards.section: Damage and replication: kinases that keep a CDK off

cards.front: After DNA damage in G1, how do the checkpoint kinases keep Cdk2 off quickly, without new gene expression?
cards.back: They trigger rapid ubiquitin-dependent destruction of Cdc25A, the phosphatase that activates Cdk2. Cdk2 keeps its inhibitory phosphate and S phase does not start.
cards.quote: The checkpoint kinases trigger rapid ubiquitin-dependent destruction of Cdc25A, the phosphatase that activates Cdk2.
cards.section: Damage and replication: kinases that keep a CDK off

cards.front: Describe the slow route by which p53 keeps a damaged G1 cell out of S phase.
cards.back: Activated p53, a transcription factor, induces the gene for p21, a CDK inhibitor. In biochemical assays, p21 blocks cyclin E-Cdk2 from phosphorylating Rb, so S phase stays off.
cards.quote: in biochemical assays p21 blocks cyclin E-Cdk2 from phosphorylating Rb, so S phase stays off.
cards.section: Damage and replication: kinases that keep a CDK off

cards.front: Isogenic human colon cancer cells with and without p21 are given DNA damage in G1. Predict the difference.
cards.back: Cells lacking p21 lose the G1 arrest after damage altogether; cells with p21 arrest. This was found in those cells, not every cell type.
cards.quote: In isogenic human colon cancer lines, Waldman, Kinzler and Vogelstein found that losing p21 abolished the G1 arrest after DNA damage altogether
cards.section: Damage and replication: kinases that keep a CDK off

cards.front: Once DNA breaks are resolved or replication is finished, how is CDK activity restored in a cell that can still recover?
cards.back: Checkpoint signalling is silenced, then phosphatases and the remaking of destroyed proteins such as Cdc25A restore CDK activity.
cards.quote: In a cell still able to recover, phosphatases and the remaking of destroyed proteins such as Cdc25A then restore CDK activity.
cards.section: Damage and replication: kinases that keep a CDK off

cards.front: What defect identified the budding-yeast mad and bub mutants?
cards.back: They kept going (failed to arrest) when a drug destroyed their microtubules. Mad: mitotic arrest deficient; bub: budding uninhibited by benzimidazole.
cards.quote: isolated budding-yeast mutants that kept going when a drug destroyed their microtubules.
cards.section: The spindle checkpoint: one kinetochore says wait

cards.front: In a PtK1 cell, one chromosome is attached to only one pole. A laser destroys its unattached kinetochore, and the chromosome stays stranded near the pole. Anaphase follows about 20 minutes later. What does this show?
cards.back: The spindle checkpoint does not check alignment. An unattached kinetochore emits a wait signal, and removing the kinetochore removed the signal.
cards.quote: It was listening to a wait signal from an unattached kinetochore, and removing the kinetochore removed the signal.
cards.section: The spindle checkpoint: one kinetochore says wait

cards.front: Unattached kinetochores promote assembly of the mitotic checkpoint complex (MCC), made of {{c1::Mad2, Cdc20, BubR1 and Bub3}}.
cards.back: The MCC holds APC/C-Cdc20 back.
cards.quote: Unattached kinetochores promote assembly of the mitotic checkpoint complex (MCC): Mad2, Cdc20, BubR1 and Bub3.
cards.section: The spindle checkpoint: one kinetochore says wait

cards.front: How does the mitotic checkpoint complex keep securin and cyclin B away from APC/C-Cdc20?
cards.back: Like a decoy key: BubR1 sequences that mimic a substrate's destruction signal sit in Cdc20's substrate-gripping slots. BubR1 also blocks the E2 enzyme UbcH10.
cards.quote: BubR1 carries sequences that look like a substrate's destruction signal, and they sit in the slots on Cdc20 that would grip a real substrate
cards.section: The spindle checkpoint: one kinetochore says wait

cards.front: An antibody that blocks Mad2 is injected into a cell in prometaphase, while some kinetochores are still unattached. Does anaphase come earlier or later, and why?
cards.back: Earlier (premature anaphase). Without Mad2 no MCC forms, APC/C-Cdc20 is free, and the wait is gone.
cards.quote: Injecting an anti-Mad2 antibody into PtK1 cells or primary human keratinocytes in prophase or prometaphase brought on premature anaphase.
cards.section: The spindle checkpoint: one kinetochore says wait

cards.front: Cells held in nocodazole, with the spindle checkpoint still active, can eventually leave mitosis. Why?
cards.back: The brake leaks: cyclin B is still slowly destroyed by a proteasome-dependent route, so the cells slip out.
cards.quote: PtK and human RPE1 cells held in nocodazole can slip out of mitosis while the checkpoint is still active, because cyclin B is slowly destroyed by a proteasome-dependent route.
cards.section: The spindle checkpoint: one kinetochore says wait

cards.front: Trace the steps from active APC/C-Cdc20 to the separation of sister chromatids.
cards.back: APC/C-Cdc20 ubiquitinates securin (and cyclin B, which in vertebrate cells must also be destroyed); the proteasome destroys them; freed separase cuts Scc1, the cohesin subunit holding sisters together; anaphase begins.
cards.quote: Freed separase cuts Scc1, the cohesin subunit that holds sister chromatids together, and anaphase begins.
cards.section: Anaphase: APC/C-Cdc20 destroys securin and cyclin B

cards.front: HeLa cells at metaphase are treated with the proteasome inhibitor MG132 after the spindle checkpoint is satisfied. Predict what happens to securin, and why.
cards.back: Securin is not broken down. APC/C only ubiquitinates it; the proteasome does the destroying.
cards.quote: APC/C is the ubiquitin ligase; the proteasome does the destroying (in HeLa cells, the proteasome inhibitor MG132 blocked securin breakdown).
cards.section: Anaphase: APC/C-Cdc20 destroys securin and cyclin B

cards.front: Why is a brake made by removing a protein harder to reverse than a brake made by phosphorylation?
cards.back: A phosphate can be removed and put back within seconds to minutes because the protein is still there. A destroyed protein comes back only by being made again.
cards.quote: A phosphate can be removed and put back within seconds to minutes, depending on the substrate, because the protein is still there.
cards.section: Why it does not run backwards

cards.front: Mitotic cells are forced out of mitosis with a Cdk1 inhibitor while cyclin B is kept intact; in other cells cyclin B is destroyed first. The inhibitor is then washed out. Predict both outcomes and the conclusion.
cards.back: Cyclin B intact: many cells return to mitosis, since Cdk1 switches back on. Cyclin B destroyed: they stay out, since Cdk1 has no partner until new cyclin is made. Destruction makes exit stick.
cards.why: Inhibitory Cdk1 phosphorylation after exit can also act as a second lock in G1.
cards.quote: Cells whose cyclin B had been destroyed before washout did not return, because Cdk1 had no partner until new cyclin was made.
cards.section: Why it does not run backwards

cards.front: What positive feedback makes entry into mitosis switch-like?
cards.back: Active Cdk1 activates its activator Cdc25 and inhibits its inhibitor Wee1, so once Cdk1 activity starts to rise, the rise feeds itself.
cards.quote: Active Cdk1 activates its activator Cdc25 and inhibits its inhibitor Wee1, so once Cdk1 activity starts to rise, the rise feeds itself.
cards.section: Feedback: the Cdk1 switch

cards.front: The Cdk1 switch is {{c1::bistable}}: over a middle range of cyclin B, it can sit stably off or on, depending on where it came from.
cards.quote: A switch like this is bistable: over a middle range of cyclin B, it can sit stably off or on, depending on where it came from.
cards.section: Feedback: the Cdk1 switch

cards.front: In the Cdk1 switch with other regulators held fixed, a mitotic cell's cyclin B falls from high to a middle level, still above the lower threshold. Is Cdk1 on or off?
cards.back: Still on. The switch turns off only below the lower threshold; the gap between thresholds gives it memory, so entering mitosis takes more cyclin B than staying in it.
cards.quote: If cyclin B is the only input varied and other regulators are held fixed, the switch turns on above an upper threshold and off below a lower one.
cards.section: Feedback: the Cdk1 switch

cards.front: A checkpoint cuts Cdc25 activity by the same amount in two cells: one in G2 with the Cdk1 switch off, one just after the switch has flipped on. Predict the effect in each.
cards.back: G2 cell: Cdk1 stays off and the cell waits. Switched-on cell: Cdk1 may stay on, because the on state is held up by its own feedback.
cards.why: This suggests why the damage brake normally acts in G2, before the switch flips.
cards.quote: a cut in Cdc25 activity that keeps an off switch off may not turn an on switch off, because the on state is held up by its own feedback.
cards.section: Feedback: the Cdk1 switch

cards.front: In budding yeast, the SCF subunit Hrt1 is inactivated. Predict what happens to the CDK inhibitor Sic1 and to the cell cycle, and why.
cards.back: Sic1 stays stable and the cells arrest at G1/S. Without SCF ubiquitination, phosphorylated Sic1 is not destroyed, so the S-phase cyclin-CDK stays off.
cards.quote: When the SCF subunit Hrt1 was inactivated, Sic1 stayed stable and cells arrested at G1/S.
cards.section: G1/S: SCF destroys Sic1

cards.front: Compare the one-way step at budding-yeast G1/S with the one at anaphase: which ligase acts, what it targets, and what that releases.
cards.back: G1/S: SCF destroys phosphorylated Sic1, releasing the S-phase cyclin-CDK. Anaphase: APC/C-Cdc20 destroys securin (freeing separase) and cyclin B (a major way Cdk1 is turned off). Both stick because destroyed proteins must be made again.
cards.quote: The same logic runs at the budding-yeast G1/S transition through a second ligase, SCF.
cards.section: G1/S: SCF destroys Sic1

cards.front: In made-up HeLa data, fluorescent securin (percent of metaphase value) is 100, 71, 50, 35 and 25 at 0, 5, 10, 15 and 20 minutes after metaphase. Assuming first-order decay and negligible synthesis, find the rate constant and half-life.
cards.quote: Suppose HeLa cells express fluorescent securin, and fluorescence (as percent of its metaphase value) is measured at 0, 5, 10, 15 and 20 minutes after metaphase: 100, 71, 50, 35, 25.
cards.section: A worked problem: timing securin destruction

cards.front: Securin in a made-up HeLa cell decays with k = 0.0693 per minute from metaphase. If sister separation waits until securin is below 10 percent, about when does anaphase begin?
cards.back: t = ln 10 / k = 2.303 / 0.0693 = about 33 minutes after metaphase.
cards.why: The data alone do not say when anaphase begins; the 10 percent threshold is an assumption.
cards.section: A worked problem: timing securin destruction

cards.front: In a variant made-up cell, fluorescent securin falls to 50 percent of its metaphase value 5 minutes after metaphase and keeps decaying exponentially. How long until it is below 10 percent?
cards.back: k = 0.693 / 5 = 0.139 per minute. t = ln 10 / k = 2.303 / 0.139 = about 16.6 minutes.
cards.why: Same first-order method as the 10-minute half-life example, which gave 33 minutes.
cards.quote: Half-life: 0.693 / 0.0693 = 10 minutes.
cards.section: A worked problem: timing securin destruction

cards.front: In the made-up securin time course (half-life 10 minutes), the spindle poison nocodazole is added at 10 minutes, when fluorescence is 50. Predict fluorescence over the next 20 minutes.
cards.back: It should stay near 50 if the checkpoint switches back on quickly: kinetochores are unattached again, the MCC holds APC/C-Cdc20 back, and destruction stops. With no stop it would reach 12.5 by 30 minutes.
cards.quote: It should stay near 50, if the checkpoint switches back on quickly.
cards.section: A worked problem: timing securin destruction

cards.front: HeLa cells express a securin with a mutated destruction box (D-box), the short sequence APC/C recognizes. Predict its fluorescence at metaphase and the effect on sister chromatids.
cards.back: It does not fall at metaphase, and sister chromatid separation is inhibited.
cards.why: It was degraded later, in anaphase, through a second APC/C recognition sequence, the KEN box.
cards.quote: A D-box mutant securin would not fall at metaphase; in HeLa cells such a mutant inhibited sister chromatid separation.
cards.section: A worked problem: timing securin destruction

cards.front: RNAi against protein Z lengthens mitosis. The delay disappears when Mad2 is also depleted, and Z-depleted cells still arrest in nocodazole. Is Z a checkpoint component or an attachment protein?
cards.back: An attachment protein. Unattached kinetochores keep signalling, so mitosis lengthens; the delay needs the checkpoint, so removing Mad2 collapses it, and the nocodazole arrest stays intact.
cards.quote: That delay should collapse if Mad2 is depleted as well, because the delay needs the checkpoint.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: RNAi against protein Z shortens mitosis, and Z-depleted cells leave nocodazole arrest. What does this suggest about Z, and what control guards against a misleading weak arrest?
cards.back: Z behaves like Mad2, a checkpoint component. Measure how long cells stay arrested, not only whether they leave, since a strong checkpoint can look weak when cells slip out by slow cyclin B loss.
cards.why: Rescue with an RNAi-resistant Z shows the effect is Z's.
cards.quote: Mitosis may get shorter, as it did after anti-Mad2 injection, and Z-depleted cells cannot stay arrested in nocodazole.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: What happens to mouse embryo cells lacking Mad2, even without spindle damage?
cards.back: They grow normally at first, but once the epiblast divides rapidly they missegregate chromosomes and die. Mad2 is needed in every cycle, not only in emergencies.
cards.quote: Mouse embryo cells lacking Mad2 grow normally at first, but once the epiblast starts dividing rapidly they missegregate chromosomes and die, even without spindle damage.
cards.section: When checkpoint proteins are needed in every cycle

cards.front: In budding yeast, MEC1 and RAD53 are essential. Deleting SML1, an inhibitor of ribonucleotide reductase, suppresses their lethality. What does this show?
cards.back: Their essential job is mainly supplying DNA building blocks (dNTPs), not making the cell wait.
cards.quote: Their lethality is suppressed by deleting SML1, an inhibitor of ribonucleotide reductase, so their essential job is mainly supplying DNA building blocks (dNTPs) rather than making the cell wait.
cards.section: When checkpoint proteins are needed in every cycle

cards.front: Cultured human cells with no added damage are treated with an ATR inhibitor during ordinary S phase. Predict their mitotic timing.
cards.back: They enter mitosis early with under-replicated DNA. ATR, activated by ETAA1, normally holds back a CDK1-driven switch on FOXM1 until S phase ends.
cards.quote: when ATR was inhibited, cells entered mitosis early with under-replicated DNA.
cards.section: When checkpoint proteins are needed in every cycle

cards.front: A human cell expresses a Cdc25A that cannot be ubiquitinated but has normal p53. It is irradiated in G1. Predict the early and later response.
cards.back: The fast G1 arrest should fail, since Cdc25A is not destroyed and keeps activating Cdk2. By inference from the two routes, a slower arrest could still come from p53 inducing p21, which blocks cyclin E-Cdk2.
cards.why: G1 has two routes: fast Cdc25A destruction with no new gene expression, and slow p53-p21 transcription.
cards.quote: This step needs no new gene expression and, in the classic experiment, no p53 (Going deeper).
cards.section: Damage and replication: kinases that keep a CDK off
